title: Castles & Knights
strapline: Raise the drawbridge — there's a dragon at the gate.
intent: A castle is a whole world in a tray: children invent kingdoms, quests and characters and keep the story running over days.
Knights, kings, dragons and villagers pull children into rich pretend talk — commands, warnings, brave speeches and rescues.
Building and rebuilding the castle walls is real early engineering: what makes a tower that won't topple?
Big themes get played out safely — danger, bravery, goodies and baddies, keeping people safe — which is how young children make sense of their own fears.
The language of long-ago slips in naturally: castle, moat, drawbridge, armour, banner, feast — and 'a very long time ago'.
implementation: Set the scene with a few strong pieces — a wooden castle, knights, horses, a dragon, some trees and small-world people — and leave room for children to add their own.
Take a bit-part role (a frightened villager, a lost traveller) so children hold the powerful roles and drive the story.
Narrate quietly alongside the play to lend words: 'The knight lowered the drawbridge and crept across the moat...'.
Offer loose parts — blocks, fabric, corks, pebbles — so the castle can be built, knocked down and rebuilt bigger.
Draw out the story with wondering, not questions: 'I wonder what's making that noise inside the tower.'
Follow a shared book or a child's dragon obsession, and let the small world become where that story gets retold and rewritten.
key_questions: Who lives in your castle, and who is trying to get in?
How will the knight keep everyone safe tonight?
How could we build the tower so it stands up tall?
What happened to the dragon — is it a baddie, or just lonely?
What might it have been like to live in a castle long ago?

impact.text: Children role-play knights, kings and dragons, acting out familiar quests and rescues.
Older children sustain an imaginative castle world over several days, with characters, storylines and rules they invent and defend.
Children tell their own castle stories — who did what, and what happened next — in a connected sequence.
Children build, topple and rebuild castle walls and towers, solving how to make them stable.
Children negotiate roles and turns in the shared world, sorting out who is the knight and who guards the gate.
Children use positional and 'long ago' language as they play — over the moat, inside the tower, in the olden days.

enhancements: Fabric, blocks and cardboard tubes for building bigger castles and adding towers.
Shiny fabric, foil and 'jewels' for treasure, crowns and armour.
A shared castle story or dragon book left beside the tray to spark retelling.
Small-world horses, a dragon, villagers and farm animals to widen the cast.
Mark-making nearby — maps of the kingdom, wanted posters, royal invitations.
A large-scale version outdoors with crates and planks so children can be the knights themselves.

playing_exploring: Children pretend on a grand scale, playing out bravery and danger where they are safely in charge.
Every new prop is tested for its part in the story — could this be the dragon's cave?
active_learning: Children return to the same castle world day after day, keeping a self-chosen story and its rules alive.
creating_thinking: Children invent their own quests, solve how to build a tower that stands, and decide how the story should end.
